📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NEW YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Egan-Jones released a commentary examining how artificial intelligence could reshape the services economy, and whether workers displaced by the technology will keep the income to buy what they want. It offers institutional investors a framework for assessing the risks.

Industry observers note that services now dominate US employment, and professional services such as accounting, audit, legal and consulting, along with software, face the most immediate effects of AI. Much of that exposure sits outside public markets: ten of the 20 largest US accounting firms are backed by private equity. As AI reprices billable work, the commentary finds disruption risk falling on partners and private equity sponsors, who hold the equity, and on the private credit funds that hold much of the debt.

Against that, Egan-Jones argues that demand is highly elastic: people buy more and expect higher quality as prices decline. It points to radiology: after AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton stated in 2016 that people should stop training radiologists, demand for scans kept climbing, and US programs offered a record 1,478 training positions this year.

Egan-Jones also expects the number of consumers to grow, as always-on AI agents effectively add buyers.

The harder question, according to the commentary, is how people will obtain capital to act on those demands if they cease to be economically useful in a world where intelligence is no longer scarce. AI makes entrepreneurship easier, yet many employed people lack the capital, skills or desire to start companies, and many fresh ventures may fail. Egan-Jones expects destitution for some workers.

That is where the commentary locates political risk. It suggests a wealth tax, under which the government takes partial ownership of assets without liquidating them, appears more viable than the old model of distributing wealth. It also recalls that earlier transitions, including the Industrial Revolution, contributed to mass revolutions and suffering in several countries. Investors are advised to watch for regulation and tax restructuring.

Egan-Jones concludes that appetite alone pays no bills: AI will hit software and services businesses, many of them in private hands, and displaced workers may lack the income to spend. Navigating this economic transition, it says, must be done cautiously.

Trump, Putin and Xi signed onto a 1985 Reagan-Gorbachev nuclear line in 90 minutes of talks — Ukraine didn’t even come up by name

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it was touted as a history-making summit of the year.
  • Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.
  • As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.

Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.

But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?

As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.

The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially upcoming global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.

It has been revealed that and then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

Recent findings suggest that it was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a major table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.

In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.

Sources indicate that so we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body.

And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”.

Recent findings suggest that all three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.

The major thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.

For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.

In a recent development, but the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.

It has been revealed that at the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the organization of Putin and Xi.

Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those complications – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.

In a recent development, there were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.

Of course, the substantial three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years.

Recent findings suggest that also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed.

Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary.

What Trump may want is detente rather than a latest Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that.

Rana Mitter, Professor of U.S.-Asia Relations, Harvard Kennedy School.

Jeff Bezos has a space firm, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder remarked he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios declared Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos remarked a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The Upcoming York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos mentioned the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”.

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he mentioned. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and claims it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and claims it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

It has been revealed that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It claims TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

Industry observers note that on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

According to recent reports, here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

Recent findings suggest that none of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

Industry observers note that the AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card states AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card indicates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a massive generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 fresh tokens and a 40,960-token context.

It has been revealed that anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

Industry observers note that the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

In a recent development, overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

According to recent reports, the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

In a recent development, FRESH YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Saturn Cloud, the inference platform for enterprises running open models, today announced a partnership with Tileward to bring its compressed open models to Saturn Cloud's token factory platform. Operators can run the same models with less GPU memory, so each GPU can serve more tokens.

It has been revealed that saturn Cloud's token factory turns GPU fleets into managed inference and fine-tuning services that operators sell to their own customers, under their own brand. Tenant isolation, quotas, metering, and enterprise governance are built in. It runs on NVIDIA Dynamo, in public cloud, private cloud, or on-premises. Serving Kimi K3 to 16 live agent sessions on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, Saturn Cloud delivered 7,380 total tokens per second per GPU at about 37 tokens per second per user, matching the SemiAnalysis InferenceX benchmark recipe on the same GPUs. Tileward's models run on this serving stack.

In a recent development, "Operators sell inference from GPUs they've already paid for, and memory is usually what runs out first," stated Sebastian Metti, Founder and CEO of Saturn Cloud. "Tileward gives that memory back, so operators can take on more customers and longer contexts with the fleet they have, without buying more GPUs.".

Tileward, a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups, offers compressed models that are up to 78% smaller than the published weights. Tileward evaluates each one against the original on benchmarks including MMLU, SWE-bench Verified, and AgentBench.

Sources indicate that "Making a model smaller was never the hard part. Proving it still gives the right answers is," mentioned Anantha Sharma, Founder and CTO of Tileward. "We publish how we measure every model, so operators on Saturn Cloud can check the quality before they sell a single token of it.".

Operators can swap in Tileward's weights for the published ones, and their serving stack, tenants, rate cards, and brand stay the same. The freed memory lets them run more copies of each model, fit large models on fewer GPUs, and serve more concurrent users with longer contexts. Serving more tokens from each GPU lowers the cost per token, giving operators more margin on input, cached, and output rates, or room to price lower.

Compressed versions of gpt-oss-120b, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash are available now to neoclouds, AI factory operators, telcos, sovereign AI providers, and enterprises running Saturn Cloud's token factory platform on their own GPUs. Contact Saturn Cloud or Tileward to add them to a deployment.

It has been revealed that saturn Cloud is the enterprise inference platform for open models and agents. Built on the NVIDIA inference stack, Saturn Cloud tunes each deployment to the customer's workload and optimizes throughput and latency to meet the contractual SLA. Enterprises run any open model or open-source agent on dedicated GPUs from Saturn Cloud's neocloud partners or inside their own networks, including air-gapped networks. GPU cloud operators use Saturn Cloud's token factory platform to sell inference from their own fleets. Learn more at saturncloud.io.

In a recent development, tileward makes open models smaller while preserving publisher accuracy and runs them as a hosted API, in a manufacturer's own cloud, or fully air-gapped. Learn more at tileward.com.

SNL’s viral ‘Sister’ sketch asks why pay for elder care when a daughter does it free — a home health aide runs about $6,688 a month

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “Sister” has gone viral.
  • 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.
  • According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “Sister” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?

The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

In a recent development, as researchers who study aging, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.

While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements.

According to recent reports, this distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately $6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

In a recent development, for many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.

Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Sources indicate that unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023. The divide between these programs dates back to 1965, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.

According to recent reports, however, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services.

Who provides care in the meantime?

Industry observers note that having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

According to recent reports, the nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born.

The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025, only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned.

When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.

Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.

Recent findings suggest that over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, Latest Jersey and about a dozen other states, for example, have released paid family leave programs. In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers. Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage.

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

Recent findings suggest that “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the concern extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.

Jane Tavares, Senior Research Fellow and Lecturer of Gerontology, UMass Boston and Marc Cohen, Professor of Gerontology, UMass Boston.

  • Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, unveiled a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, unveiled a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company looks to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, remarked Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he remarked. “We have to take newly introduced technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Industry observers note that batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The manufacturer must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

Industry observers note that the firm has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round revealed in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Recent findings suggest that seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Recent findings suggest that group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced prepares for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky mentioned.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Industry observers note that most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Industry observers note that denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

In a recent development, timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

According to recent reports, this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

According to recent reports, node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Sources indicate that finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

Recent findings suggest that this is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

According to recent reports, the affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams blueprint to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

Recent findings suggest that the coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Industry observers note that denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

Industry observers note that two latest bonus episodes of the Connected Nation podcast take on both complications. Connected Nation (CN), a national nonprofit, interviewed leadership at SHLB and Google during the Broadband Nation Expo taking place in New Orleans Nov. 18-20.

Industry observers note that joseph Wender, Executive Director of the Schools, Health & Libraries Broadband (SHLB) Coalition, explained the Fifth Circuit ruling that puts the $8 billion-a-year program at risk. The court found that USAC, which runs the Universal Service Fund, was improperly set up.

Google and the Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) are building it with more than 90 companies, and it's expected in early 2027 (Q1).

Tozzi also explained why some suppliers face as many as 50 audits a year, and what really goes into building a data center.

It has been revealed that "We need to go at hyper speed because we need it fast," Tozzi stated of developing the standard. "We couldn't afford to wait three or five years.".

#18621. Grand Theft Auto made crime a game. AI is doing the same for hacking

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (830 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Grand Theft Auto made crime a game. AI is doing the same for hacking

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that fans have waited 13 years for Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • Sources indicate that six days before the launch, the FBI issued a FLASH warning about ARTEX, an open-source tool that lets AI agents carry out an intrusion “at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.” Some attacks reached privileged access in under three hours.
  • Rockstar knows what a bored teenager can do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that fans have waited 13 years for Grand Theft Auto VI. The wait for GTA V’s sequel dragged on through so many delays that it became a meme. When a game takes that long, you’d expect it to feel dated on arrival. But when GTA VI finally arrived this week, the opposite thing happened. The real world has started to look a lot like the game.

Sources indicate that six days before the launch, the FBI issued a FLASH warning about ARTEX, an open-source tool that lets AI agents carry out an intrusion “at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.” Some attacks reached privileged access in under three hours. The GitHub repository has since been taken down, but copies are still out there, and it has already been used against banks, government agencies, and tech companies. Skill, time, and money used to separate a bored teenager from a professional crew. Now a bored teenager with AI can operate like one.

Rockstar knows what a bored teenager can do. In 2022, a 17-year-old broke into the company and leaked early GTA VI footage from a hotel room, using an Amazon Fire Stick and a phone. That took some serious skills and marked the last time anyone would need them. Rockstar spent 13 years building a game that feels like real life. In the same stretch, real life took on the rules of the game. AI turned the hacking craft into a criminal loop. You pick a target, try, fail, try again, at almost no cost, with the push of a button, from your couch. While developing the latest GTA took more than a decade, reality caught up in a fraction of that.

That shift left defenses behind, because they were built for a slower pace. Attackers now run on three-hour clocks, while most security programs run on fiscal years. The best attacks don’t look like attacks at all. They arrive as job offers, invoices, calendar invites, and logins that look almost normal. Meanwhile, defenders are being asked to move faster and to tell real from fake at the same time.

When the first GTA VI trailer came out, half of the internet asked the same question. Is this gameplay or real footage? Corporate security teams ask that every day now. In September, a Binance engineer went through two rounds of interviews for what looked like a great job and downloaded the take-home assignment. It was malware. The FBI blamed North Korea, and Binance puts the theft that followed at about $6.3 billion. A day after Microsoft 365 went down this month, attackers were already exploiting the confusion, sending fake outage notices that cited the real incident number.

Industry observers note that now look at how slowly most companies change their defenses. Adopting a new approach means a six-month evaluation, a few more months to roll it out, and a pilot that waits for next year’s initiative. I understand the caution, because security leaders have been burned by tools that promised a lot and broke things in production. But an attack that moves at machine speed doesn’t wait for procurement. Attackers are playing on easy mode, and the defense is stuck on a loading screen.

The obvious answer is to make defense faster, and speed does matter. But fast and wrong is still wrong. A team that misreads that signal will shut down its own business over a broken router, while the real attack walks in looking like a job offer. Making the right call takes context that even the best AI model doesn’t have on its own, like who owns the server, whether that user really logged in from Lisbon, and what breaks if a system goes offline. That context lives inside your manufacturer, and defense only works when your AI agents know it too.

The leaders I see handling this well have changed three things.

Know the business first. Before buying more detection, they make sure their defenses understand which systems matter, who relies on them, and what normal looks like. AI can’t tell an attack from a failure without that context.

Sources indicate that save the caution for what can’t be undone. Ending one session can be reversed in minutes, so it can happen right away, within rules the team sets. Decisions that can’t be taken back get a closer look and a person’s sign-off.

It has been revealed that change in weeks, not quarters. They try agentic defense early, measure how often it gets real cases right, and give it more room as it earns trust.

In a recent development, in GTA, players can reload their last save. Security teams don’t have that luxury. Companies that make the right call at machine speed will still be around for the next GTA installment, however long it takes.

Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • It has been revealed that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • In a recent development, loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path reveals how far the probing went.

It has been revealed that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

In a recent development, loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, claims user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction highlights a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

According to recent reports, the numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

Industry observers note that that arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

In a recent development, the harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

According to recent reports, that detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

According to recent reports, loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale claims its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

Recent findings suggest that so the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team notes it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

In a recent development, loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

According to recent reports, the two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

Recent findings suggest that the takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Industry observers note that vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

Industry observers note that this looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem reveals pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin mining giant MARA Holdings, formerly known as Marathon Digital, continues to offload its Bitcoin holdings, with another multimillion-dollar transfer spotted as the company's selling spree reveals no signs of slowing down.

It has been revealed that according to blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, MARA transferred another 366 BTC, worth approximately $23.33 million, from its wallets on Nov. 18.

The latest transaction follows a series of substantial Bitcoin sales by the mining company throughout 2026.

Lookonchain estimates that MARA has already sold a staggering 40,581 BTC this year, generating approximately $3.03 billion at an average selling price of $74,446 per coin.

However, it remains unclear whether the latest 366 BTC transfer represents another completed sale or an internal movement of funds.

MARA's aggressive selling strategy is confirmed by its latest quarterly financial disclosures.

According to its Nov. 9 SEC filing, the company sold approximately 26,984 BTC for $1.9 billion during the first nine months of 2026.

Following the end of September, MARA liquidated another 13,597 BTC at an average price of approximately $81,039, raising an additional $1.1 billion.

These transactions bring its total disclosed Bitcoin sales to 40,581 BTC.

Notably, the tech giant used $750 million from its latest sales to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans, releasing 17,477 BTC previously pledged as collateral.

Interestingly, MARA has explicitly signaled that it intends to continue selling Bitcoin as part of a broader shift in its corporate strategy.

However, it began allowing sales of newly mined Bitcoin in 2025 before expanding the policy in 2026 to include coins already held on its balance sheet.

In its latest shareholder letter, MARA stated it looks to continue monetizing Bitcoin to strengthen its financial flexibility.

The tech giant specifically identified artificial intelligence infrastructure, upcoming convertible debt obligations and potential share repurchases as reasons for building up cash reserves.

The selling comes as MARA faces considerable pressure on its core mining business.

Third-quarter revenue declined 35% year over year to $164.2 million, compared to $252.4 million in the corresponding period of 2025.

#18615. Gen X’s $2.3 trillion caregiving curse: I’m the sister from John Mulaney’s SNL skit and I did the math

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (898 w)

Gen X’s $2.3 trillion caregiving curse: I’m the sister from John Mulaney’s SNL skit and I did the math

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on Saturday Night Live this weekend, John Mulaney sold America its oldest elder-care product.
  • The joke lands because it isn’t one, particularly the part about finances.
  • It has been revealed that earlier this month, AARP released a report, built on the Urban Institute’s long-range income model, estimating that the typical working caregiver will lose $120,500 over her lifetime in wages, workplace retirement income and Social Security.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Saturday Night Live this weekend, John Mulaney sold America its oldest elder-care product. “Sister,” his pitchman explains, is a live-in, 24/7 caregiver who is “completely free, and also your sister.” Mikey Day’s Dr. Grant, author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care, explains how it works: years of internalized sexism have convinced her that caring for Mom and Dad is her job and somehow not yours. The best part, another brother adds, is that the parents drew up the will before she moved in, so you still get half the house she’s deep cleaning. Within a day, the sketch had 2 million views on YouTube, and women all over the country were sending it to their brothers.

The joke lands because it isn’t one, particularly the part about finances. It’s impossible to create or maintain wealth while caregiving.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, AARP released a report, built on the Urban Institute’s long-range income model, estimating that the typical working caregiver will lose $120,500 over her lifetime in wages, workplace retirement income and Social Security. Across a single generation of caregivers, those born in the early 1980s, the losses come to $2.3 trillion. And that study counts only caregivers who kept their jobs. The sister in the sketch, the one who moved in, isn’t in that number. Her losses are larger because the damage doesn’t end when the caregiving does. Social Security calculates benefits from a worker’s 35 highest-earning years, and every year without a paycheck goes into that average as a zero. A woman who leaves work for five years to care for a parent doesn’t just lose five years of income. She locks in a smaller check for the rest of her life, long after the person she cared for has died.

In 2024, America’s 59 million family caregivers provided 49.5 billion hours of care, work the AARP Public Policy Institute values at $1.01 trillion, more than total Medicaid spending that year. Three in five of those caregivers are women. But the trillion-dollar figure measures only what the care is worth. It says nothing about what the care costs the person giving it, or where that money ends up. The will joke does. It is the most precise line of economic analysis anyone has delivered on caregiving this year: she does the work, and the family’s wealth is split as if she hadn’t.

Meanwhile, she is spending down whatever she had. AARP’s 2026 out-of-pocket study, released in October, found that caregivers now spend an average of $11,508 a year on caregiving, nearly 60 percent more than in 2021 and about 31 percent of household income. Caregivers who retired earlier than planned spend more, $18,940 a year. Most of it goes to housing, food and medical bills: the mortgage on the parents’ house, the groceries, the copays. Research cited by the TIAA Institute found that nearly a quarter of caregivers have less than $1,000 saved for retirement. Caregiving doesn’t just stop a woman from building wealth. It eats the wealth she already had.

Her lost wages are a leave policy her employer never had to fund. Her unpaid hours are home-health services the state never had to buy. Her savings pay down the expenses of a household that isn’t legally hers. And her labor keeps her parents out of a nursing home, which keeps their house and savings from being spent on one. That intact estate is then divided, often equally, among children who did not do the work. The brothers in the sketch aren’t only getting their weekends back. They’re getting their raises, their 401(k) matches, their full Social Security records, and half the house.

According to recent reports, this is why caregiving is so rarely described as a financial arrangement, and so often described as love. Calling it love settles the accounts in advance. No one owes her anything, because what she gave was a gift. Employers that face no leave costs, governments that avoid paying for home care, and siblings who get back to “my life and the stuff I like to do” all benefit from keeping it that way. The rhetoric of priceless care conveniently treats it as worthless.

Some of the fixes are already written. The Social Security Caregiver Credit Act, reintroduced in April by Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy and Upcoming York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, would credit caregivers who provide at least 80 hours of care a month with up to five years of deemed earnings, so that those years stop counting as zeros. Congress should pass it, and extend it. Caregiving should earn retirement contributions, not just retirement credits. States can pay family caregivers through Medicaid at real wages, not token stipends. And families can do what the law doesn’t require: put the caregiving into the will. A sibling who gave years of labor to keep the estate intact has contributed to it, and an even split that ignores that contribution isn’t fair. It’s a transfer from her to everyone else who retires on full pensions and she retires on a three-digit Social Security check, in an apartment, while the house she cleaned for years is sold and split down the middle.

Tech Report: ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle firm talked about building for years but always found too major to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting newly introduced software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle firm talked about building for years but always found too major to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting newly introduced software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” noted Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how significant we’re willing to dream.”.

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The manufacturer has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy stated there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

In a recent development, annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The firm isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

It has been revealed that pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The latest products take that approach further:.

Recent findings suggest that to decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Industry observers note that duffy stated he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” mentioned Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

According to recent reports, both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy noted.

According to recent reports, AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

It has been revealed that plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he stated.

In a recent development, “This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy remarked. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

It has been revealed that bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Sources indicate that neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy noted.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Recent findings suggest that pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy mentioned no launch in the manufacturer’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

It has been revealed that the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Recent findings suggest that duffy stated Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

It has been revealed that despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the organization, Duffy remarked Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy stated Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

#18609. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1598 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FinCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • In a recent development, MEXC says user assets remain secure.
  • On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

FinCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

In a recent development, MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

In a recent development, on the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange claims it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

In a recent development, two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

Industry observers note that on Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN claims MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Recent findings suggest that iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN claims the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary consumers anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

Recent findings suggest that one provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

In a recent development, for most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how people or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

Recent findings suggest that finCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Industry observers note that three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.
