#18608. Tech Report: From LA to Memphis, 10 massive US jails share one strain

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3050 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: From LA to Memphis, 10 massive US jails share one strain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • WorldAtlas ranks the 10 largest US jails, but court delays, paperwork lags and disputed counts mean their headcounts keep shifting.
  • The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department runs the biggest jail operation in the country.
  • According to recent reports, the latest change came from California voters, not from the county.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WorldAtlas ranks the 10 largest US jails, but court delays, paperwork lags and disputed counts mean their headcounts keep shifting.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department runs the biggest jail operation in the country. It is a network of jails rather than a single building, and Men's Central Jail and the Twin Towers Correctional Facility are its largest pieces. WorldAtlas reports that the system holds about 19,836 people daily, far more than the 13,849 it counts at Rikers Island in New York. A newer local figure puts that lead in doubt. The Los Angeles Daily News reports that the county's jails hold about 12,500 people today. On that count, Los Angeles would hold fewer people than the Rikers figure, so its claim to the biggest jail depends on which count a reader uses and when it was taken. Either way, the people who set that number mostly work outside the jail walls.

According to recent reports, the latest change came from California voters, not from the county. Voters passed Proposition 36 in 2024, and the surge in arrests that followed pushed the county's jail population up to a peak of about 13,500, according to the . Los Angeles County had no separate say in that vote, and voters across the whole state can refill a jail system the county is trying to empty. The added people entered jails that were already struggling with crowded housing, with the care of people who are mentally ill and with the use of force inside.

According to recent reports, worldAtlas ranks the Rikers Island complex in New York City second among the country's biggest jails, holding about 13,849 people. That rank rests on a headcount that more recent reporting does not match. By November 2026, the city held about 6,700 people on the island, according to The Associated Press. If the lower count holds, Rikers Island is a much smaller jail than its rank suggests. The gap fits a city that is working to empty the jail, and on Rikers Island the falling population is the main fact to watch.

Newly introduced York City officials treat the number of people on Rikers Island as the obstacle to closing it, not as capacity to manage. The Associated Press that Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan aims to bring the population down to a little over 4,000. Even the lower current count sits well above that goal. The city has to reach that smaller population before it can replace the island with jails in the boroughs. Every person kept out of Rikers Island brings the closure closer, and the size of the jail measures how far the city still has to go.

Industry observers note that worldAtlas estimates that Maricopa County's jail system near Phoenix, which spans several facilities, holds 9,265 people. That estimate makes it one of the largest jail populations in the country. The deadliest problem in the system is the drugs that reach the people inside. Drug-related causes killed more people in Maricopa County's jails in 2025 than every other cause combined, accounting for 20 of the 39 deaths in custody there that year, according to AZFamily.

Recent findings suggest that people held in Maricopa County's jails die far more often than people held in other major urban jail systems. "In the case of Chicago and Newly introduced York City, they’re a quarter the rate of deaths that we have here in Phoenix in the Maricopa County system," criminologist Andy Hall AZFamily. Hall is comparing rates, not totals. Maricopa County's large population cannot account for the gap, and the size of the system does not explain those deaths.

Industry observers note that metro West Detention Center in Miami is Miami-Dade County's largest jail, and WorldAtlas reports that it averages about 7,050 inmates, more than Dallas County holds in its jail. A county count puts that figure in doubt. The county's corrections department put the jail's population at 2,332 as of January 2023, according to NBC 6 South Florida. On that count, Metro West would fall well short of Dallas. One figure is an average, and the other is the latest count the department had given in early 2023, so neither settles the jail's size. Even the smaller count was the highest of any Miami-Dade jail at the time.

The jail's size is in dispute, but the rise in force inside it is not. Officers at Metro West used force 380 times in 2022, up from 198 in 2019, according to NBC 6 South Florida. Miami-Dade Public Defender Carlos Martinez, whose office defends people held in the county's jails, traced the trouble inside them to how the county pays and staffs its guards. "We have a serious toxic mix because they are not paying enough to the guards, and therefore, people are not even applying to become guards, and therefore you have a lot of officers spending overtime," Martinez remarked in 2023. If he is right, the county could ease part of the pressure inside Metro West by changing what it pays officers.

Recent findings suggest that cook County, Ill., cut the size of its jail through deliberate policy choices. Even after that cut, the county holds about 6,294 people in Cook County Jail in Chicago, according to WorldAtlas, enough to rank eighth among the country's largest jails. In the early 2010s, the county routinely held more than 10,000 people there, so the jail today holds far fewer people than it once did. Releasing more people before trial was one of the policy changes behind the decline. Most people in the jail have not yet had their day in court, and that made pretrial release a policy that could reach a large share of its population.

According to recent reports, releasing people before trial did not end the jail's role as a place that holds people with mental illness. When the jail's daily count stood at 9,000, about a third of those inside were living with a mental health condition, according to the . The county has moved many people out before trial, and the ones still held are more and more likely to need serious care. Those people remain in the custody of the Cook County Sheriff's Office, which runs the jail.

Sources indicate that the Shelby County Sheriff's Office runs the downtown jail in Memphis, Tenn., and WorldAtlas estimates that it holds 5,765 people. That estimate ranks the jail 10th among the largest in the U.S. Sheriff Anthony Buckner gives a much smaller number. FOX13 Memphis reports that he put the population at more than 2,700 during a Sept. 1, 2026, tour. Neither count settles how many people the county holds there today, and the correct one determines whether Shelby County runs one of the country's very largest jails or a much more modest one. Its place on the list is best read as provisional.

In a recent development, on either count, the jail has little or no room to spare. It was built for about 2,800 people, according to . The sheriff's count comes close to that limit, and the WorldAtlas estimate goes far beyond it. When nearly every bed is in use, staff have few places to move people if part of the building fails. This building has been in service for more than 40 years, and in June its air conditioning broke down in a major outage.

The officials who run America's massive jails and the lawyers who fight them tend to agree that these places have too many people in them. A jail is where people wait for a court date, for a transfer to prison or for release, and in the largest jails thousands of people are waiting on any given day. The complaint about that crowding comes from both coasts and from both sides of the courtroom. Fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani calls the scale of imprisonment a problem for the whole country, according to The Associated Press. In Houston, defense attorney Andino Reynal claims his county locks up far more people than it needs to, according to KPRC Click2Houston. When an elected official in one city and a defense lawyer in another make the same complaint, a big jail's headcount is worth reading as a possible sign of strain rather than only as a measure of what a county can handle.

The number of people in a major jail depends both on how many people come in and on how promptly courts and clerks' offices move them back out. What speeds or slows each of those steps differs from county to county, so two jails of similar size can be full for very different reasons. Because those forces change, a county can see its jail population rise or fall by thousands of people within a few years, and officials in several counties now report counts far from earlier estimates. When a jail holds more people than it was built or staffed for, the people held inside and the county taxpayers who fund it both bear the cost.

Sources indicate that worldAtlas set out to rank the largest jails in the U.S. by the number of people held in them, a group that includes Rikers Island in New York, Harris County's jail in Houston, Maricopa County's jails in Phoenix, and Shelby County's jail in Memphis, Tenn. Each figure reflects one moment in a situation that keeps changing, in counties working to shrink their jails and in counties struggling to find room.

The county wants to shrink the system enough to close Men's Central Jail. The Los Angeles Daily News reports that the closure would require a population far below today's, which means moving thousands of people out rather than a few hundred. The sheriff runs the buildings, but judges decide who leaves them. "Neither the Court nor the County can predetermine or guarantee that particular individuals will be diverted, released, or otherwise handled in a manner that advances specific population reduction targets," noted David Slayton, executive officer of the Los Angeles County Superior Court.

It has been revealed that new York City has bound itself to a deadline it cannot meet. The city is legally required to close Rikers Island and replace it by 2027, The Associated Press reports, but the mayor's initiative sets the closure for 2032, the year the last replacement jail, in Manhattan, is expected to open. The city cannot empty the island until its final replacement exists, and it cannot speed up construction by decision alone. Meanwhile, conditions inside have brought in a federal court. The New York City Department of Correction runs Rikers Island, but a federal judge has appointed an outside manager there. The court's step highlights that the trouble lies in how the jail is run, not only in how many people it holds.

Roughly 10,000 people spend each day in the Houston jail run by the Harris County Sheriff's Office, a total that places it third in the nation, according to WorldAtlas. That count still leaves out some of the people the county detains. Harris County holds more people than its own jail can take, and it sends the rest to other places. More than 900 Harris County inmates are held in private facilities, KPRC Click2Houston reports, and some of them are housed as far away as Louisiana. The jail's own headcount therefore understates how many people Harris County detains.

Recent findings suggest that the crowding began in the courts, not in the jail. The sheriff's office, which runs the jail, traces the overcrowding to cases that piled up in the county courts after Hurricane Harvey and then the COVID pandemic, according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office statement reported by KPRC Click2Houston. If the sheriff's office is right, the jail is likely to stay crowded until judges work through those delayed cases.

Recent findings suggest that sending people away costs the county more than keeping them in its own jail. Holding someone in an outside private facility costs an average of $91 a day, compared with $53 in the county jail, according to KPRC Click2Houston. The county pays for that overflow from its main budget, and a delay in the courtroom has become a standing expense for the county.

Recent findings suggest that the county has tied itself to outside beds for years, not months, under a contract that runs until 2028, according to KPRC Click2Houston. At least one of the officials who oversee the deal is uneasy about it. "This is one of those things that keeps me up at night," Harris County Commissioner Lesley Briones said of the contracts.

Recent findings suggest that jail officials have tried to stop drugs at the door, but the deaths have continued. They added body scanners and fresh drug-detection dogs, according to AZFamily, and four people still died in two weeks at Lower Buckeye Jail, between late June and the July 4 weekend. In Hall's view, the jail's own staff are one of the main ways drugs get inside. If he is right, screening the people who come through the entrance may not be enough to keep drugs out.

Curran-Fromhold Correctional Facility, Philadelphia's main intake jail, holds an estimated 8,811 inmates, enough to place it among the half-dozen largest jails in the country, according to WorldAtlas. As the main intake jail, it is where Philadelphia receives people into its jail system. Most readers would expect a population that size at a sprawling county network, yet this estimate belongs to a single city facility. On paper, a figure that large would make one Philadelphia building as busy as some entire county systems.

The size of the building argues against reading that estimate literally. Curran-Fromhold has room to house about 2,000 people, and the population figure is only an approximation. Nothing on record settles which of those numbers describes the jail on a given day. There is no evidence that thousands of extra people are crowded into its beds, and none that the larger figure counts people held anywhere else. The jail earns its place among the nation's largest on a rough estimate.

It has been revealed that no one at Metro West lost a job as the use of force rose. No staff member there was fired for using force in the three years through early 2023, according to NBC 6 South Florida. The higher count does not show that officers acted wrongly in any single case. It does show that the jail's discipline record stayed the same while officers used force far more often.

According to recent reports, dallas County, Texas, holds its place among the country's biggest jails by a very slim margin, keeping about 6,385 people in its jail, slightly more than Cook County does, according to WorldAtlas. With so little room between the two, neither position should be read as settled. The Dallas count also captures a population that keeps shifting. The county recently kept its jail below 6,775 people a day for a month, which was its longest stretch under that level in more than a year, according to The Dallas Morning News. Dallas's rank reflects the moment the jail was counted more than any fixed size.

Some of the people in Dallas County's cells are waiting on documents, not on a judge. When a case ends, the jail needs paperwork from the clerks before it can release or transfer the person. Those papers reached the jail 20 days after a case ended, on average, in 2025, according to The Dallas Morning News. Part of the jail's headcount therefore depends on how fast the county handles its own paperwork.

The delay also costs taxpayers, and the county is trying to stop it where the paperwork starts. The Commissioners Court has approved at least $450,000 in payouts since 2024 to resolve civil rights claims by people kept in jail beyond their release dates, according to The Dallas Morning News. The county's answer is to get judgments right the first time. "If we don't get the judgment done correctly at first it doesn't matter how efficient we are on the backend because it's going to be kicked back," Steven Autry, Dallas County director of judicial and corrections operations, told The Dallas Morning News.

The change depends on the people behind it as well as on the process. The Dallas Morning News reports that District Attorney John Creuzot, whose office helped push for the new approach, lost his race for another term and will step down in January.

According to recent reports, in Orange County, Calif., one agency answers for everyone the county locks up. The Orange County Sheriff's Department runs the jail as a network of buildings rather than a single jailhouse. Three of its sites are in Santa Ana: the Intake Release Center and separate central jails for men and for women, while a fourth, the Theo Lacy Facility, is in the city of Orange. On a typical day, the department holds around 6,000 people across those sites, the ninth-largest jail population in the U.S., according to WorldAtlas. That total is better understood as people than as a rank. Each of those people depends on the sheriff's department for medical care and physical safety, and the department's responsibility grows with every person booked in.

In Orange County, the cost of holding that many people demonstrates up in what happens to them inside. The concerns raised about the system center on deaths in custody, the medical care detainees receive, and the force used against them. Keeping people alive, treating them when they are sick and not harming them are the most basic duties the sheriff's department owes everyone it holds. Those three concerns go to the core of that duty, and they are a truer test of a system this large than its place among the country's biggest jails.

Putting off repairs on an old, full jail doesn't save the county money. Instead, the bill grows when something breaks. "We know that if maintenance goes untouched, then it becomes crisis management and it becomes crisis maintenance. And we know that when we're in those states, it costs way more money than to make repairs when you're in a crisis state," Buckner told FOX13 Memphis. County taxpayers pay that higher bill, and the people held inside live with each breakdown until the repairs are made.

MEXC confirmed that its Global Card service will be discontinued on November 18, according to the exchange's announcement. The company cites service adjustments by its third-party card issuer. From the deadline, existing cards can no longer be used for transactions, and new card applications are suspended.

Customers have two things to take care of before the service ends.

First, the remaining card balance has to be withdrawn: the Withdraw button on the Global Card page sends the funds to the Fiat account.

In a recent development, second, subscriptions linked to the card should be cancelled or switched to another payment method. Unfortunately for cardholders, recurring payments will most likely fail if they stay on the old card.

According to recent reports, if there's still a balance when the service ends, MEXC will credit it to the Spot account, so people will simply receive their funds back. It's crucial to keep in mind that pending card transactions need time to settle, which is why the balance snapshot comes on November 21, three days after the shutdown. The amount will be credited within three business days of the snapshot. Users do not need to take any action.

It has been revealed that refunds for previous card transactions will be credited to the Fiat account once MEXC receives them. Pending cashback will be credited automatically as scheduled. Elite VVIP consumers with zero-fee benefits will be refunded too, though the eligible fees return to their Spot accounts only before December 15.

Transaction history, card orders and cashback records stay available on the Global Card page for three months after the service ends, so it's worth saving anything needed before access ends.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain types of services to third parties all the time, so witnessing a similar situation is more than a possibility here. Realistically, the shutdown is somewhat inconvenient rather than dangerous, as the balances are returned automatically. For people: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

‘It might be too tough’: Trump second-guessed his immigration crackdown after the midterms. Then his Labor Department doubled down

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after a blue wave in the November midterms, President Donald Trump told CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Nov.
  • His administration just doubled down anyway.
  • In a recent development, “I think I got an A plus for closing up the border.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after a blue wave in the November midterms, President Donald Trump told CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Nov. 8 that his immigration crackdown “might be too tough.”.

His administration just doubled down anyway. On Nov. 17, the Labor Department proposed an overhaul of the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, the step most employers have to clear before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card. Companies would face longer recruitment campaigns and a two-year bar on filing after laying off U.S. workers in similar jobs, and occupations in short supply, including nurses, would lose their exemption from the standard labor market test. For companies that sponsor foreign hires, that means more time, more paperwork and more ways to get turned down. The Labor Department received 117,849 PERM applications in fiscal 2025, down 22.4% from the year before.

In a recent development, “I think I got an A plus for closing up the border. I got very high marks for getting the bad ones out,” Trump stated. “But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation of breaking the law—and that was that they came into the country illegally.”.

According to recent reports, “I think it might be too tough, yeah,” Trump continued, regarding his immigration policy. “And a lotta people would say that it’s great. But a lotta people think it’s too tough.”.

And Trump has made the case for foreign workers before. In an interview with Fox News in November 2025, Trump conceded that the U.S. needs foreign labor due to domestic workers lacking “certain talents.”.

In a recent development, “You also do have to bring in talent,” Trump said. “We don’t have talented people here. You don’t have certain talents, and you have to. People have to learn.”.

The White House and Donald Trump did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune.

Recent findings suggest that under the existing system, employers generally have to obtain Labor Department certification demonstrating that there are not enough qualified and available U.S. workers for a particular position—meaning hiring a foreign worker won’t negatively affect wages and working conditions for domestic workers. The employers typically use the process to sponsor foreign laborers for employment-based green cards.

But the proposed changes would require employers to conduct more extensive recruitment campaigns, eliminate administrative exemptions and prohibit employers from filing PERM applications for positions in the same or similar occupations for two years after laying off domestic workers in those same roles. The department is also proposing to extend recruitment advertising periods to at least 90 days and impose additional documentation and reporting requirements on employers.

The consequential part of the proposal lands on the bypass standards—which have allowed certain occupations to be exempt from the standard labor market test if the roles were in need of workers. The standard requirement would be extended to occupations that are in short supply—including professional nurses and scientists of “exceptional ability.”.

But Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said these changes would ensure American workers will receive priority for high-skilled, high-paying positions.

“American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said in a press release. “This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labor.”.

And in May, USCIS issued a policy memorandum introducing guidance that would also make it harder for foreign workers already living in the U.S. to obtain green cards without leaving the country. The memorandum emphasizes that adjustment of status is a “discretionary decision” over an automatic entitlement. Essentially, eligible immigrants already in the U.S. that can apply for lawful permanent residency through USCIS are not guaranteed.

“Given the significant privileges granted to lawful permanent residents, USCIS reminds its officers that they must consider and weigh all the relevant evidence in the record,” the memo read, “taking into account the totality of the circumstances to determine whether the alien is suitable for permanent residence and if approval of the alien’s adjustment of status application is in the best interest of the United States.”.

The Trump administration also tightened employment-based green card sponsorship in September 2025, with an imposed $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa applications.

“The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a press release.

Industry observers note that comments on the proposal are due Jan. 19, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that in its latest update on the investigation, ULA remarked it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, ULA stated early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

According to recent reports, the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the tech giant looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

Recent findings suggest that the finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Upcoming Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn releases reserved for Leo.

According to recent reports, ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA remarked.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

Cardano-based stablecoin DJED has announced its sunset, as DJED and SHEN services will wind down on December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC.

DJED represents a crypto-backed, overcollateralized stablecoin protocol on Cardano whose US-dollar peg is maintained algorithmically against an ADA reserve (with SHEN as the reserve coin), rather than by fiat reserves.

"DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC," a DJED-focused X account wrote.

Sources indicate that ATTN: DJED & SHEN Holders DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026 at 11:59pm UTC. Please redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN you hold before then. All redemptions are subject to the reserve ratio.

Recent findings suggest that users are urged to redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN they hold before this deadline. Users are to redeem on the protocol and convert their DJED and SHEN back to ADA on the official Djed page. Users who hold DJED or SHEN in liquidity pools, lending markets, or other DeFi platforms are urged to withdraw those positions first, then redeem or swap.

The Djed team noted all systems are fully operational and redemptions are now open, subject to the reserve ratio. It further added that the Djed protocol will be maintained and remain available until December 31, 2026. After this date, all remaining funds will be allocated to the outstanding DJED/SHEN holders once the wind-down is complete.

Djed’s shutdown comes almost three years after its launch, which came in 2023. The stablecoin was officially launched on the Cardano mainnet on January 31, 2023, and was developed by COTI in collaboration with the Cardano ecosystem to be used on DeFi protocols on Cardano as a stable alternative to volatile cryptocurrencies.

In positive news for the Cardano ecosystem, Monument Bank Limited has launched tokenized deposits on the Midnight network, marking a milestone for the network and the decentralized finance ecosystem.

At present, Monument is the first UK bank to tokenize retail deposits on a public blockchain, offering clients a 5.2% AER fixed-term return on savings directly through its existing banking app, delivering institutional onchain finance through a familiar and user-friendly banking experience.

Up to £250 million of client deposits will be represented on Midnight in this opening phase, with deposits recorded one-to-one in sterling.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

Industry observers note that the White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

It has been revealed that the abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets claims it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

It has been revealed that review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

Industry observers note that "Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

Sources indicate that the SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ notes a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move promptly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Sources indicate that crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

Sources indicate that the sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

It has been revealed that the package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, even in 1979, the year of the Iranian revolution, gas lines and Paul Volcker, American inflation never got above 15%.
  • In a recent development, A meaningful slice of Americans expects prices to rise faster than that over the next year anyway.
  • Industry observers note that the typical household is far calmer, and getting calmer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, even in 1979, the year of the Iranian revolution, gas lines and Paul Volcker, American inflation never got above 15%. It peaked just below that level in early 1980 before Volcker’s rate hikes broke it, according to the Federal Reserve’s own history. Prices haven’t risen faster than 15% a year since 1947.

In a recent development, A meaningful slice of Americans expects prices to rise faster than that over the next year anyway. “Almost 15% of consumers expect (or claim they expect) inflation of over 15%,” UBS chief economist Paul Donovan wrote in a Nov. 20 note titled “The benign inflation scenario.” In the University of Michigan’s October survey, 16% of consumers mentioned prices would rise 15% or more over the next year, about the same share as a year earlier, according to the survey’s own tables.

Industry observers note that the typical household is far calmer, and getting calmer. Median year-ahead inflation expectations “plunged from 4.7% last month to 3.7% this month,” University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers director Joanne Hsu stated in the final November reading released Friday. That gap between the most frightened consumers and the data is what anyone setting prices or pay should watch. In the late 1970s, expectations that came loose from the numbers ended up feeding the inflation.

It has been revealed that since the government’s consumer price records begin in 1913, 12-month inflation has cleared it in only two stretches: on and off from 1917 to 1920, peaking at 23.7% in June 1920, and from November 1946 to June 1947, after World War II price controls came off, according to BLS data compiled by the St. Louis Fed and the BLS’s own history of the index.

To hit 15% next year, prices would have to rise about four times as fast as the 3.7% they rose in the 12 months through September.

Consumers “tend to expect future inflation that is higher than official estimates of current inflation,” Fed economists wrote in a 2016 note, in part because they remember price increases more readily than cuts and weight the things they buy most often. They also feel price levels, not rates: grocery prices were up more than 27% from five years earlier as of early 2025, the Minneapolis Fed noted, even as the inflation rate itself had cooled.

Partisanship matters, too, Michigan’s survey team has found. Independents’ inflation expectations “have consistently been closer to the political party not in the White House,” Michigan’s survey team found in 2024, and survey director Joanne Hsu mentioned “the overwhelming size and persistence of the partisan gap has generated substantial economic uncertainty.”.

Voters have already said what they think of prices. About 9 in 10 midterm voters called the cost of living a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress, and about 6 in 10 of them backed Democratic House candidates, according to the AP Voter Poll of roughly 100,000 voters. Republicans took a blistering set of losses in House, Senate and governor’s races, AP reported. About two-thirds of voters said President Trump’s policies had fueled inflation; in 2022, only about half said the same of President Biden’s, AP reported.

It has been revealed that everyday costs weighed hardest. About 6 in 10 voters stated they were “very concerned” about food and grocery costs, according to AP’s analysis of the poll, and about 1 in 5 said inflation had caused their family severe hardship, according to CBS News exit polls. Among voters earning less than $50,000, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off than two years earlier.

Industry observers note that americans have braced for price spikes before. In May 2008, with gas at records, Michigan’s year-ahead expectations jumped to 5.2%, the highest since February 1982, CNBC reported. Inflation did climb, to 5.6% in July 2008. Then the financial crisis hit, and by July 2009 prices were 2.1% lower than a year earlier, per BLS data.

Industry observers note that the bigger miss came last year. Tariff announcements pushed Michigan’s year-ahead expectations to 6.5% in April 2025, the highest since 1981, with 60% of respondents volunteering comments about tariffs, the Boston Globe reported; the preliminary May reading hit 7.3%, before the final came in at 6.6%, per the University of Michigan. Actual inflation that April was 2.3%.

This time the median isn’t the outlier. Michigan’s typical household now expects 3.7%, the same rate as September’s actual inflation.

Sources indicate that in 1979, the Iranian revolution cut output by 4.8 million barrels a day, about 7% of world production, and oil prices more than doubled between April 1979 and April 1980, per the Fed. This year it’s the Iran war. Brent crude is up more than 60% from before the fighting and briefly topped $117 a barrel in late October, Al Jazeera reported. U.S. diesel hit records in September. Gasoline was up 37.4% in the 12 months through October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

According to recent reports, those are the prices people see every week, and they drive what households expect. Donovan’s argument is that U.S. median inflation “has been falling to near pre-pandemic norms,” while the visible costs, airfares and diesel-driven shipping, come from the Iran war. Airline fares rose again in October, per BLS.

In a recent development, fed researchers have tracked this pattern for decades. A 2016 Fed note found households hear more news about prices when gas prices swing hard; in 1979, a year when gas rose around 20% or more, more than 10% of households reported hearing bad news about rising prices.

According to recent reports, back then the inflation was everywhere. Consumer prices rose 13.3% in 1979 and 12.5% in 1980. This October, BLS mentioned prices rose 0.4% for the month, with core prices up 0.3%. It couldn’t publish an annual rate, because it collected no prices in October 2025, when the government shut down. Bank of America estimates the rate at about 3.8% headline and 2.7% core.

Recent findings suggest that michigan’s median household expected 9.7% inflation in both 1979 and 1980, according to the 2016 Fed note. Boston Fed researchers Philippe Andrade and Michael Wicklein found in 2025 that the 1978–80 surge in expectations was “much larger than the increase that rising prices usually would imply.” More than 5 percentage points of it couldn’t be explained by actual prices at all; gasoline accounted for about one point. They call it the de-anchoring of expectations, and it’s what Volcker spent the early 1980s grinding out.

In a recent development, the central bank is the other difference. The fed funds rate went from 10% at the start of 1979 to 19% by the middle of 1981, per the St. Louis Fed, and unemployment topped 10%. This Fed raised rates a quarter point in September, then held them at 3.75% to 4% at its Oct. 28 meeting, with two officials voting for another hike.

In 1979, the typical household’s 9.7% guess was, if anything, too low; inflation came in at 13.3%. Donovan’s slice of consumers is expecting more than the Volcker era ever delivered, while the median household now expects 3.7%. The next read on who’s right is the November consumer price index, due Dec. 10.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, remarked on Friday that he believes he has proven the Riemann hypothesis with help from the company's Claude AI model.

It has been revealed that "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Alpöge wrote in a statement on his website. No outside experts have reviewed the proof, according to AFP.

Alpöge posted the proof in Lean, a formal coding language in which a computer can confirm each stage of an argument in sequence. The AI-written version runs more than 250,000 pages, according to The Wall Street Journal. He noted his approach also settles the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a more sweeping formulation of the same question, according to AFP. He plans to write up the full argument.

It has been revealed that bernhard Riemann proposed the hypothesis in 1859. It deals with how prime numbers are spread out. The Clay Mathematics Institute named it one of seven Millennium Prize Problems in 2000, each carrying a $1 million award. By the institute's criteria, a claimed solution needs a peer-reviewed publication and must then hold up for two further years of examination, according to AFP.

"If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, told Scientific American.

Recent findings suggest that alpöge stated the result arrived as Sunday evening rolled over into Monday, a few days ahead of Anthropic's IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. He called the timing "horrible" and sent CEO Dario Amodei a note requesting approval to make the news public. "The fact is that there was a constraint to respect," Alpöge wrote. Anthropic stock slid during its first full session on the market, and the company did not respond to a request for comment, according to The Wall Street Journal and AFP.

Anthropic disclosed in August that an unreleased Claude model had advanced a long-standing finding tied to the Riemann hypothesis without proving it, according to AFP.

The claim follows OpenAI's September announcement that it had claimed a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize Problem. A credit dispute followed. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at Fresh York University, accused OpenAI of racing ahead after it learned of related work he had posted with Alpöge a day earlier. OpenAI said it never saw their work.

Industry observers note that in October, OpenAI posted 722 papers claiming answers to open problems, including advances on the Riemann hypothesis. The firm pulled three papers within days after finding errors, and noted the results were "at different stages of verification.".

Considering the history of the transferred funds, the move has sparked speculation that the hacker might already be preparing to spend the stolen funds, further sabotaging Binance’s chances of full recovery.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives people access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.

Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.

The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.

The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image.

Sources indicate that “Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.”.

The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot.

Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives.

While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like.

In a recent development, “For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang noted. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.”.

Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms.

The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives.

“We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia said. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.”.

Xia said beta customers were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later.

Industry observers note that “We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang said. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.”.

In terms of funding, the firm raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year.

Phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Recent findings suggest that sister will provide. True, French Gates stated, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Recent findings suggest that paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers remarked they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates remarked Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

It has been revealed that she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

Industry observers note that in its own analysis, The Fresh York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After decades of playing a doctor on the long-running medical drama ER and today’s The Pitt, Noah Wyle has learned a thing or two about what it’s like to be a health care professional and the challenges patients face.

Now, he is taking that passion off-screen, partnering up with popular scrubs maker Figs with a goal to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt in the U.S.

According to recent reports, “In my countless interactions with health care professionals over the decades, one thing that stays with me is how they try to do everything right for a patient while the system makes it harder than it should be,” Wyle said in a statement. “Medical debt follows people home, creates long-term devastation, and changes the whole experience of care.”.

Americans owe at least $220 billion in medical debt, according to a 2024 KFF-Peterson analysis of federal survey data, and having insurance offers less protection than many assume. In a newly introduced Urban Institute study backed by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, more than one-quarter of U.S. adults said they or a family member owed medical debt at the end of 2025, including 26% of those with health coverage. Hospitals were the most common creditor.

It has been revealed that separately, a Commonwealth Fund survey released in September found that roughly one in three working-age adults with private insurance are paying off medical bills over time, with some pulling from savings or spending less on food and rent to keep up. The matter has also come up on-screen in Wyle’s indicates. In one episode of The Pitt, a construction worker who already owes $100,000 in medical bills lands in the ER with serious diabetes complications after rationing his insulin because he can’t afford it.

“Trust is the bedrock of the relationship between patients and clinicians like nurses, pharmacists, and doctors, and that trust is increasingly undermined by the burden, and even fear, of medical debt,” Allison Sesso, president and CEO of nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, said in a statement.

During the next three years, Wyle and Figs will each donate $1 million to Undue Medical Debt, which wipes out, on average, $100 of qualifying medical debt for every $1 donated. The commitment is projected to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt for over 150,000 Americans. The first round of relief is set to take place in time for the upcoming holidays, according to the release.

It has been revealed that wyle, Figs, and Undue Medical Debt over the same time frame will work to develop and share practical resources for health care professionals to help patients navigate affordability. This builds on Figs’ and Wyle’s broader “Healthcare Is Human” advocacy work, focused on addressing systemic pressures making it challenging for health care workers to care for their patients.

“This is an act of half philanthropy and half protest, to underscore what the need is, and see if we can’t get our arms around some better solutions,” Wyle told CNN.

Wyle also serves as Figs’ global brand ambassador and has joined the tech giant on Capitol Hill to push for policies supporting health care workers. He wore the brand’s first black-tie scrubs to the Emmy Awards last year.

Figs, a publicly traded firm cofounded by CEO Trina Spear, reported third-quarter revenue of $190.7 million earlier this month, up nearly 26% from a year earlier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a fresh AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Confirmed Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

In a recent development, nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar claims its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds upcoming matches as creators become more popular.

It has been revealed that once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”.

In a recent development, another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a newly introduced baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.

Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The firm aims to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.

This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit.
  • ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains.
  • It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, noted it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, noted it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and challenges shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration indicates how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 latest shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

In a recent development, yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:.

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with consumers urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't strategy around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a proposal as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For consumers, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

According to recent reports, terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the organization’s experimental arm, unveiled the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

It has been revealed that howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Industry observers note that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

In a recent development, consumers cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it released publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

According to recent reports, the deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of people. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

In a recent development, for years, I thought I knew what separated my moving company from others. I’m a fourth-generation mover and have worked in this industry professionally since I was 18. My father always mentioned moving was in my blood — hence our name, Can’t Quit Moving. I built my business on lessons passed down through my family: Work hard, treat people and their belongings with respect and do the job the right way. After hearing countless moving horror stories from customers, I knew we operated differently.

According to recent reports, and I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience. I certainly didn’t see our everyday work as content, as something other people would want to know more about or as something that could help grow the manufacturer. That changed when someone from outside the industry spent a day with us.

According to recent reports, during the pandemic, a good friend of mine who worked as a cameraman was out of work, so he joined our crew for a day. At the end of it, he climbed into the truck looking rattled. “That was a crazy day,” he told me. My response: “That was a Tuesday.”.

Every day, we dealt with closing delays, low bridges, furniture that wouldn’t fit, last-minute additions and customers navigating one of the most stressful days of their lives. To me, that was second nature. To him, it was a story, and he told me we needed to film it.

That eventually became an unscripted docuseries about our company, but it also changed how I thought about growing a business. Until then, we had relied solely on word of mouth. What I hadn’t realized was that showing people what sets us apart from the competition could become a growth strategy.

In a recent development, when you spend every day doing the same thing, you lose sight of what makes it interesting. I didn’t think twice about the problems we encountered on a move, because solving them was my job. But to an outsider, the process was wild. Parking and loading our truck, for example, fascinated our cameraman. It made me realize that the work my team and I do takes real skill.

In a recent development, that’s something business owners in any industry can overlook. You don’t need a glamorous product or a business built for social media to have a story worth telling. A contractor solving a job site problem, a restaurant prepping for a Saturday night or a bookseller opening their store all have something customers rarely get to see.

Simply put, your best content could already be happening. You just have to recognize and document it.

Sources indicate that when we started filming, I had to unlearn some of my business owner instincts. After our second day, my wife paused a piece of footage and asked what I had been thinking in that moment. The truth was, I had been thinking plenty. I just wasn’t saying it.

According to recent reports, I was trained to stay calm even when things went off the rails. My wife told me to talk to the camera like I was talking to my best friend. I had to rewire my thinking: Explain the problem. Share what you’re thinking. Admit when you’re frustrated. Just be real.

That taught me the difference between advertising and real storytelling. Business owners spend a lot of time telling customers who they are: We’re trustworthy. We care. We go above and beyond. And so on.

Documenting our work allowed us to show those things instead. Our motto is “We take the stress out of your move,” and now people could see that firsthand: how our crew wraps belongings to protect them from torrential rain, how we responded when a move didn’t go as planned because of an insurance headache and how we treated customers even when we were close to pulling our hair out under high-pressure deadlines. The messy moments highlighted more about the company than the camera-ready ones.

Other entrepreneurs can learn from this. What do you claim about your business that you could demonstrate instead?

Recent findings suggest that after we finished filming the show, a former customer who worked in the film industry encouraged us to start sharing our story on social media. Creating content consistently has sometimes felt like starting another business, but it also changed how I think about marketing. Traditional advertising usually tries to reach someone around the time they’re ready to buy. Telling a story and building an audience can create a relationship long before that.

Sources indicate that that’s especially important in a business like moving. People don’t need movers every month. Someone might discover one of our videos today and not move for another year. But if they keep following the company and seeing our crew at work, we don’t have to introduce ourselves when they’re finally ready for a quote. The audience comes first. The customer can come later.

Industry observers note that and we’re starting to see that play out. When we ask latest customers how they found us, more and more of them mention our videos. One man contacted us about moving his lemon trees because he’d seen us move palm trees on Instagram. During another move, a customer’s 6-year-old recognized us from our YouTube Shorts. To me, that was proof: People weren’t just remembering our moving tech giant. They were remembering us. They felt like they’d gotten to know the people behind the business, and more importantly, they already trusted us.

In a recent development, don’t get me wrong: You don’t need to create a docuseries to apply this strategy. I’d start with three questions:.

Recent findings suggest that the goal isn’t to capture someone’s attention for the sole purpose of selling something. That’s empty, and it doesn’t build trust. The point is to give viewers, your potential customers, a reason to keep paying attention.

It has been revealed that your competitors can offer similar services. They can lower their prices and make the same claims about why they’re better. What they can’t replicate is your people, your experiences, your perspective and how you do your work.
